content: The intervention group, which received a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol, demonstrated a lower rate of failed expulsion compared to the group that received misoprostol alone. However, the certainty of this evidence is low. A higher proportion of women in the mifepristone plus misoprostol group achieved a complete abortion without requiring surgical intervention compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. The combination of mifepristone and misoprostol resulted in fewer complications necessitating uterine aspiration compared to misoprostol alone. The certainty of this evidence is high. Women in the mifepristone plus misoprostol group experienced fewer side effects such as chills, diarrhea, and severe cramping compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of evidence is high for chills and diarrhea, and moderate for severe cramping. A greater number of women in the mifepristone plus misoprostol group expressed satisfaction with their treatment compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is high. However, more women in the mifepristone plus misoprostol group experienced bleeding that required transfusion compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is low. The mifepristone plus misoprostol group also had a higher incidence of serious adverse events, such as infections, compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of this evidence is low. Side effects such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and fever were more common in the mifepristone plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-only group. The certainty of evidence ranges from moderate to high. For medical management compared to expectant management, fewer women in the medical management group experienced failed expulsion at all follow-up points. The certainty of this evidence is high. A higher proportion of women in the medical management group achieved a complete abortion without surgical intervention at 2, 7, 14, and 31 days of follow-up compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate to high. Fewer women in the medical management group experienced complications requiring uterine aspiration compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. Fewer women in the medical management group experienced complications leading to hospitalization compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of this evidence is very low. Side effects such as bleeding leading to emergency room visits, headache, dyspepsia, vomiting, and shorter bleeding duration were less common in the medical management group compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of evidence is high for headache, moderate for vomiting and bleeding duration, and low for emergency room visits and dyspepsia. More women in the medical management group expressed satisfaction with their treatment compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. The rates of blood transfusion were comparable between the medical and expectant management groups. The certainty of this evidence is very low. The occurrence of fever as a side effect was similar between the medical and expectant management groups. The certainty of this evidence is low. However, more women in the medical management group experienced side effects such as vaginal bleeding, spotting, menstrual cramping, abdominal cramping, nausea, and diarrhea compared to the expectant management group. The certainty of evidence is moderate for vaginal bleeding and nausea, and low for spotting, menstrual cramping, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. For surgical management compared to medical management, fewer women in the surgical group experienced failed expulsion. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. A higher proportion of women in the surgical group achieved a complete abortion without additional surgical intervention compared to the medical/expectant group. The certainty of this evidence is very low. Fewer women in the surgical group experienced complications requiring surgical evacuation compared to the medical/expectant group. The certainty of this evidence is high. Fewer women in the surgical group experienced complications requiring transfusion or hospital admission compared to the medical/expectant group. The certainty of evidence is very low for transfusions and moderate for admissions. Side effects such as nausea, diarrhea, pain, and bleeding were less common in the surgical group compared to the medical/expectant group. The certainty of evidence is moderate for nausea and diarrhea, low for pain, and very low for bleeding. More women in the surgical group expressed satisfaction with their treatment compared to the medical/expectant group. The certainty of this evidence is moderate. The rates of uterine perforation were comparable between the surgical and medical/expectant groups. The certainty of this evidence is very low. However, more women in the surgical group experienced failed expulsion compared to the expectant group. The certainty of this evidence is low. The cost of treatment was noted in one study, with medical management costing approximately $80. There is important uncertainty or variability in how much people value the main outcomes of these interventions. The resource requirements for these interventions are considered moderate. The cost-effectiveness of the interventions does not clearly favor either the intervention or the comparison. The impact on health equity is uncertain but is likely to have no significant impact. The acceptability of the interventions to key stakeholders is likely high. The feasibility of implementing these interventions is considered moderate.
